title: Slow, cached, or blocked?

glossary.note: Waiting includes network round-trip time and server response preparation.
Response headers control whether browser code may read a cross-origin response.

key_points: A long wait for the first byte is different from a long download.
304 validates a stored response; a memory-cache hit avoids that round trip.
A CORS failure can block script access even when a server responds.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: A page feels slow. Open Network. These timings are illustrative, not a production capture.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Five segments: lookup, connect, encrypt, wait, download. Look at the long one: waiting for the first byte.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Time to first byte covers the network round trip and server work. A long wait alone cannot prove a slow database.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Now encryption. The browser pays it once per new connection, so later requests on it show zero here.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Next, the stylesheet. The browser holds a copy and asks if it is current, sending its entity tag in If-None-Match.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Three-oh-four: not modified. No body is sent, and the browser reuses its stored copy after one short round trip.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The logo comes from memory cache. While that response is fresh, no request leaves the browser.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: One cross-origin fetch turns red. Cross-Origin Resource Sharing decides whether page script may read a response.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: The response has no Access-Control-Allow-Origin, so the browser hides it from script. The server did answer.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: This last request never finishes. It stays pending, with no status and no headers to read.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Select each request before blaming the network. Waiting, cache reuse, blocked reads, and hangs need different fixes.
